# Formal specification of the Bayesian additive multilevel model {#apx-math}

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

Let $y_i$ denote the mean EEG signal for observation $i$, with known standard error $s_i$, participant $j[i]$, condition contrast $c_i$, condition label $g_i \in \{1,2\}$, and time $t_i$. The model can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_i &\sim \operatorname{Normal}\left(\mu_i,\sqrt{\sigma^2 + s_i^2}\right) \\[4pt]
\mu_i
&=
\alpha
+ a_{j[i]}
+ \left(\beta + b_{j[i]}\right)c_i
+ f_{g_i}(t_i)
+ h_{g_i,j[i]}(t_i) \\[4pt]
\begin{bmatrix}
a_j \\
b_j
\end{bmatrix}
&\sim \operatorname{MVNormal}
\left(
\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
0
\end{bmatrix},
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
\right) \\[4pt]
\boldsymbol{\Sigma} &= \mathbf{S}\mathbf{R}\mathbf{S} \\[4pt]
\mathbf{S} &=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_a & 0 \\
0 & \sigma_b
\end{bmatrix}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, $\alpha$ is the population-level intercept, $\beta$ is the population-level condition effect, and $a_j$ and $b_j$ are participant-level deviations in intercept and condition effect (i.e., varying intercept and slope). The function $f_g(t)$ represents the population-level temporal trajectory for condition $g$, whereas $h_{g,j}(t)$ represents the participant-specific smooth deviation from that population trajectory. The residual scale combines the estimated residual standard deviation $\sigma$ with the known standard error $s_i$ of each participant-level mean.

The population-level condition-specific smooths can be represented using basis functions as

$$
f_g(t_i)
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M}
w_{gm} B_m(t_i),
$$

where $B_m(t_i)$ are spline basis functions and $w_{gm}$ are condition-specific spline coefficients. Participant-specific smooth deviations can analogously be written as

$$
h_{g,j}(t_i)
=
\sum_{m=1}^{M_j}
u_{gjm} B^{(j)}_m(t_i),
$$

where $u_{gjm}$ are participant- and condition-specific spline coefficients. Their magnitude and smoothness are controlled by penalisation parameters estimated hierarchically from the data. The priors follow the default `brms` specification:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &\sim \operatorname{Student}\text{-}t(3,0,2.5) \\[4pt]
\beta &\sim \operatorname{flat} \\[4pt]
\sigma &\sim \operatorname{Student}\text{-}t^+(3,0,2.5) \\[4pt]
\sigma_a, \sigma_b &\sim \operatorname{Student}\text{-}t^+(3,0,2.5) \\[4pt]
\sigma_{\text{smooth, pop}} &\sim \operatorname{Student}\text{-}t^+(3,0,2.5) \\[4pt]
\sigma_{\text{smooth, participant}} &\sim \operatorname{Student}\text{-}t^+(3,0,2.5) \\[4pt]
\mathbf{R} &\sim \operatorname{LKJ}(1).
\end{aligned}
$$

The superscript $+$ indicates truncation to positive values. The correlation matrix $\mathbf{R}$ describes the correlation between participant-level intercepts and condition effects.

\newpage

# Application to 2D time-resolved decoding results (cross-temporal generalisation) {#apx-2D}

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

We conducted a cross-temporal generalisation analysis of the decoding data from @nalborczyk:inprep, in which we assessed the performance of classifiers trained and tested at various time points of the trial [@king2014]. This analysis was performed at the participant level, resulting in a 2D matrix where each element contains the decoding accuracy (ROC AUC) of a classifier trained at time point $\text{training}_{i}$ and tested at time point $\text{testing}_{j}$ for each participant (@fig-timegen).

```{r fig-timegen, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, dpi = 300, fig.width = 8, out.width = "75%", fig.cap = "Group-level average cross-temporal generalisation matrix of decoding performance [data from @nalborczyk:inprep]."}

# Import the MEG decoding data
library(reticulate)
use_condaenv("r-reticulate3", conda = "~/miniforge3/bin/conda", required = TRUE)
np <- import("numpy")
data <- np$load("data/group_level_decoding_4l_2s_vs_7l_2s_visual_blocks_temporal_generalisation_all.npy")

# Convert to R array
data_r <- py_to_r(data)

# Original time vector (before decimation)
time_points <- seq(from = -0.5, to = 1.0, length.out = dim(data_r)[2])

# Remove the first 300 ms before stimulus onset
start_idx <- which.min(abs(time_points - (-0.2) ) )
end_idx <- which.min(abs(time_points - 1.0) )

# Subset data_r to keep only time points between -0.2s and 1.0s
data_cut <- data_r[, start_idx:end_idx, start_idx:end_idx]

# update time vector accordingly
time_points_cut <- time_points[start_idx:end_idx]

# Decimation factor
decim <- 4

# Select every 4th time point
data_cut_decim <- data_cut[, seq(1, dim(data_cut)[2], by = decim), seq(1, dim(data_cut)[3], by = decim)]

# Retrieve the number of participants, time points
n_participants <- dim(data_cut_decim)[1]
n_times <- dim(data_cut_decim)[2]

# Define a time vector (if not already defined)
time_points <- seq(from = -0.2, to = 1.0, length.out = n_times)

# Convert array to long format using `as.data.frame.table`
timegen_data <- as.data.frame.table(data_cut_decim)

# Rename and convert indices
colnames(timegen_data) <- c("participant", "train_idx", "test_idx", "auc")

timegen_data <- timegen_data %>%
    mutate(
    participant = as.integer(participant),
    train_idx = as.integer(train_idx),
    test_idx = as.integer(test_idx),
    train_time = time_points[train_idx],
    test_time = time_points[test_idx]
    ) %>%
    select(train_time, test_time, auc, participant) %>%
    filter(participant < 11)

# Visualise the cross-temporal generalisation matrix
timegen_data %>%
    summarise(auc = mean(auc), .by = c(train_time, test_time) ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = train_time, y = test_time, fill = auc) ) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) + 
    coord_fixed() +
    scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", midpoint = 0.5, name = "AUC") +
    labs(x = "Testing time (s)", y = "Training time (s)")
```

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

To model cross-temporal generalisation matrices of decoding performance, we extended our initial BGAM to take into account the bivariate temporal distribution of AUC values, thus producing naturally smoothed estimates (time courses) of AUC values and posterior odds. This model can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{AUC}_{i} &\sim \mathrm{Beta} \left(\mu_{i}, \phi\right)\\
\operatorname{logit} \left(\mu_{i} \right) &= \alpha + f \left(\text{train}_{i}, \text{test}_{i} \right)\\
f \left(\text{train}_{i}, \text{test}_{i} \right) &\equiv \sum_{k=1}^K b_{k} B_{k}\left(\text{train}_{i}, \text{test}_{i} \right)
\end{aligned}
$$

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

where AUC values are assumed to follow a $\mathrm{Beta}$ distribution, parametrised by a mean $\mu_{i}$ and a precision parameter $\phi$. The mean $\mu_{i}$ is linked to the predictors through a logit link function. The smooth function $f(\text{train}_{i}, \text{test}_{i})$ represents a two-dimensional surface defined over training and testing times, which captures how decoding performance varies across the temporal generalisation matrix. This surface is approximated by a linear combination of $K$ basis functions $B_{k}(\cdot, \cdot)$, each weighted by a coefficient $b_{k}$. The basis functions are constructed using a tensor product of univariate splines (here thin-plate splines) applied to the training and testing time dimensions [@wood2003; @wood2017].

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

We fitted this model using `brms` and the `t2()` tensor product smooth constructor with full penalties [@pedersen_hierarchical_2019; @wood2017]. We ran four MCMCs to approximate the posterior distribution, including each 3,000 iterations and a warmup of 1,000 iterations, yielding a total of 8,000 posterior samples to be used for inference.

```{r gam-timegen, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, results = "hide"}

# Fit a GAM with two temporal dimensions
timegen_gam <- brm(
    auc ~ t2(train_time, test_time, bs = "ps", k = 20, full = TRUE),
    data = timegen_data,
    family = brms::Beta(),
    warmup = 1000,
    iter = 3000,
    chains = 4,
    cores = 4,
    threads = threading(threads = 2),
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9),
    backend = "cmdstanr",
    stan_model_args = list(stanc_options = list("O1") ),
    file = "models/timegen_gam_meg_t2_ps_k20_full.rds"
    )
```

```{r gam-timegen-show, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE, results = "hide"}

# Fit a GAM with two temporal dimensions
timegen_gam <- brm(
    # 2D thin-plate spline (tp) with full penalties
    auc ~ t2(train_time, test_time, bs = "tp", k = 30, full = TRUE),
    data = timegen_data,
    family = Beta(),
    warmup = 1000,
    iter = 3000,
    chains = 4,
    cores = 4,
    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9)
    )
```


\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

@fig-gam-timegen-post-preds shows the model predictions (left) together with the region identified by thresholding the posterior odds (right). The model could be extended to a multilevel bivariate GAM by including participant-specific smooths, for example:

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
t2(
    train_time,
    test_time,
    participant,
    bs = c("tp", "tp", "re"),
    m = 2,
    full = TRUE
    )
```

```{r fig-gam-timegen-post-preds, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, cache = TRUE, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Predicted AUC values with threshold (left) and posterior odds of decoding accuracy being above chance (right) according to the bivariate BGAM."}

# Define a function to plot posterior predictions
plot_post_timegen <- function (
    model,
    data = NULL,
    chance_level = 0.5,
    sesoi = 0,
    thresholds = c(10, 100),
    n_draws = 1000L
    ) {

    if (is.null(data) ) {
        
        data <- model$data
        
    }

    # Complete training x testing grid
    preds_conds <- tidyr::crossing(
        train_time = sort(unique(data$train_time) ),
        test_time = sort(unique(data$test_time) )
        )

    # Use a manageable subset of posterior draws
    posterior_samples <- brms::posterior_epred(
        object = model,
        newdata = preds_conds,
        ndraws = min(as.integer(n_draws), brms::ndraws(model) )
        )

    n_draws_used <- nrow(posterior_samples)

    posterior_mean <- colMeans(posterior_samples)

    posterior_probability <- colMeans(
        posterior_samples > (chance_level + sesoi)
        )

    # bound probabilities according to the actual number of sampled draws,
    # avoiding odds equal to zero or infinity
    epsilon <- 1 / (n_draws_used + 1)

    posterior_probability_bounded <- pmin(
        pmax(posterior_probability, epsilon),
        1 - epsilon
        )

    prediction_summary <- preds_conds %>%
        mutate(
            auc = posterior_mean,
            post_prob = posterior_probability,
            prob_ratio =
                posterior_probability_bounded /
                (1 - posterior_probability_bounded)
            )

    empirical_summary <- data %>%
        summarise(
            auc = mean(auc),
            .by = c(train_time, test_time)
            )

    fill_limits <- range(
        c(prediction_summary$auc, empirical_summary$auc),
        na.rm = TRUE
        )

    # do not let the returned ggplot objects retain the large matrix/model
    rm(
        posterior_samples,
        posterior_mean,
        posterior_probability,
        posterior_probability_bounded,
        model,
        data
        )
    
    invisible(gc() )

    post_preds_plot <- prediction_summary %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = test_time, y = train_time, fill = auc) ) +
        geom_tile() +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_abline(
            slope = 1,
            intercept = 0,
            linetype = 2,
            linewidth = 0.5
            ) +
        geom_contour(
            aes(z = prob_ratio),
            breaks = thresholds,
            colour = "black",
            linewidth = 1
            ) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) +
        scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) +
        coord_fixed() +
        scale_fill_scico(
            palette = "vik",
            midpoint = 0.5,
            name = "AUC",
            limits = fill_limits
            ) +
        labs(
            x = "Testing time (s)",
            y = "Training time (s)"
            )

    prob_above_chance_plot <- prediction_summary %>%
        ggplot(
            aes(
                x = test_time,
                y = train_time,
                fill = prob_ratio
                )
            ) +
        geom_tile() +
        geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.5) +
        geom_abline(
            slope = 1,
            intercept = 0,
            linetype = 2,
            linewidth = 0.5
            ) +
        scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) +
        scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0) ) +
        coord_fixed() +
        scale_fill_scico(
            palette = "vik",
            midpoint = 1,
            name = "Posterior odds",
            trans = "log10"
            ) +
        labs(
            x = "Testing time (s)",
            y = "Training time (s)"
            )

    # post_preds_plot + prob_above_chance_plo
    combined_plot <- (
        post_preds_plot |
        prob_above_chance_plot
        ) +
        patchwork::plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1) )
    
    # Return the combined figure
    combined_plot
    
}

# Compute the SESOI as the baseline upper 99% quantile
baseline_upper_quantile <- timegen_data %>%
    filter(train_time < 0 & test_time < 0) %>%
    summarise(quantile(x = auc, probs = 0.99) ) %>%
    pull()

# Compute predictions and posterior odds contours
post_preds_plot <- plot_post_timegen(
    model = timegen_gam,
    data = timegen_data,
    chance_level = baseline_upper_quantile,
    sesoi = 0,
    thresholds = 10
    )

# Show the plot
post_preds_plot
```

# How to choose the GAM basis dimension? {#apx-basis}

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

There is no universal recommendation for choosing the optimal value of `k`, as it depends on several factors, including the sampling rate, preprocessing steps (e.g., signal-to-noise ratio, low-pass filtering), and the underlying neural dynamics of the phenomenon under investigation. A practical strategy is to choose $k$ sufficiently large that the basis dimension does not artificially constrain the smooth, and then assess its adequacy using posterior predictive checks and sensitivity analyses. Alternatively, models with different values of $k$ can be compared using predictive criteria such as LOO. We illustrate this approach below.

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

@fig-choose-k presents the posterior predictions and two forms of posterior predictive checks (PPCs) for each GAM fit using different numbers of basis functions ($k \in \{5, 10, 20, 40, 80\}$). With the exception of the $k=5$ model, all other fits yield satisfactory PPCs, indicating that the predicted data closely resemble the empirical observations. However, model comparison using the leave-one-out information criterion (LOOIC), as summarised in @tbl-k-results, identifies the $k=40$ model as the best-performing one in terms of LOOIC, closely followed by the $k=80$ model. Future simulation studies could further investigate how such model selection criteria relate to the precision of onset and offset estimates.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-k-results
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Model comparison using leave-one-out cross-validation. Models are arranged by the difference in expected log-pointwise density (ELPD) to the best model (i.e., $k = 40$)."

# Import the models
gam_models <- readRDS("results/gam_k_models.rds")

# Extract the already-computed LOO objects
loo_list <- list(
    "gam_k5"  = gam_models[["5"]]$criteria$loo,
    "gam_k10" = gam_models[["10"]]$criteria$loo,
    "gam_k20" = gam_models[["20"]]$criteria$loo,
    "gam_k40" = gam_models[["40"]]$criteria$loo,
    "gam_k80" = gam_models[["80"]]$criteria$loo
    )

# Compare the LOO objects
models_comp <- loo::loo_compare(x = loo_list)

models_comp_df <- as.data.frame(
    x = models_comp,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )

# Format the table
models_comp_df %>%
    dplyr::select(
        model,
        elpd_diff,
        se_diff,
        p_worse
        ) %>%
    rename(k = model) %>%
    mutate(
        k = str_extract(k, "\\d+")
        ) %>%
    gt() %>%
    fmt_number(
        columns = everything(),
        decimals = 2
        ) %>%
    cols_align(
        align = "right",
        columns = everything()
        ) %>%
    tab_options(
        table.width = gt::pct(40),
        table.align = "center",
        table.font.size = 12,
        latex.use_longtable = TRUE,
        quarto.disable_processing = TRUE
        )
```

        plot_post_preds(model = gam) +
        ggplot2::ggtitle(paste("Posterior predictions (k =", k_value, ")") )

        brms::pp_check(

            type = "dens_overlay"

            y = "Density"

    plots_to_combine[[plot_index + 2L]] <-
        brms::pp_check(
            gam,
            ndraws = 500,
            type = "stat_2d",
            stat = c("mean", "sd")
            ) +
        ggplot2::labs(
            x = "Mean",
            y = "SD"
            ) +
        ggplot2::ggtitle(paste("Mean vs. SD (k =", k_value, ")") )
    
    plot_index <- plot_index + 3L
    
}

# validate before combining
valid_plots <- vapply(
    plots_to_combine,
    function (x) inherits(x, "ggplot") || grid::is.grob(x),
    logical(1)
    )

if (!all(valid_plots) ) {
    
    stop (
        "Invalid plot objects at positions: ",
        paste(which(!valid_plots), collapse = ", ")
        )
    
}

final_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(
    plotlist = plots_to_combine,
    ncol = 3,
    nrow = 5,
    byrow = TRUE
    )

# `R` package and integration with `MNE-Python` {#apx-package}

\thispagestyle{fancy}

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

For readers who are already familiar with `brms`, the recommended pipeline is to use the code provided in the main paper (available at <https://github.com/lnalborczyk/brms_meeg>). It is also possible to call functions from the `neurogam R` package (available at <https://github.com/lnalborczyk/neurogam>) which come with sensible defaults.

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
library(neurogam)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# Install the neurogam package from CRAN
# install.packages("neurogam")

# Install the latest development version from Github
# remotes::install_github("https://github.com/lnalborczyk/neurogam")

# Load the package
library(neurogam)

# Fit the BGAMM and identify clusters using the testing_through_time() function
gam_results <- testing_through_time(
    # dataframe with M/EEG data in long format
    data = df,
    # the *_id arguments are used to specify the relevant columns in data 
    participant_id = "participant", meeg_id = "eeg",
    time_id = "time", predictor_id = "condition",
    # posterior odds threshold for defining clusters
    threshold = 10,
    # number of warmup MCMC iterations
    warmup = 1000,
    # total number of MCMC iterations
    iter = 5000,
    # number of MCMCs
    chains = 4,
    # number of parallel cores to use for running the MCMCs
    cores = 4
    )

# Print and visualise the results
summary(gam_results)
plot(gam_results)
ppc(gam_results)
```

\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}
\setlength{\parskip}{6pt}

The `neurogam` package can also be called from `Python` using the `rpy2` module, and can easily be integrated into `MNE-Python` pipelines. For example, we use it below to estimate the onset and offset of effects for one EEG channel from an MNE evoked object. The code used to reshape the `sample MNE` dataset is available in the online supplementary materials, and we further refer to the [MNE documentation](https://mne.tools/stable/auto_tutorials/epochs/50_epochs_to_data_frame.html) about converting `MNE` epochs to `Pandas` dataframes in long format (i.e., with one observation per row).

```{python, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# loading the Python modules
import mne
from mne.datasets import sample
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# defining the path to the "sample" dataset
path = sample.data_path()

# loading the evoked data
evokeds = mne.read_evokeds(path / "MEG" / "sample" / "sample_audvis-ave.fif")

# defining a function to reshape the data
def reshape_eeg_channels_as_participants(evokeds, condition_labels):
    
    all_dfs = []

    for evoked, condition in zip(evokeds, condition_labels):
        
        # selecting only EEG channels
        picks = mne.pick_types(evoked.info, meg=False, eeg=True)
        data = evoked.data[picks, :]
        channel_names = np.array(evoked.ch_names)[picks]

        n_channels, n_times = data.shape
        # repeating time for each channel
        times = np.tile(evoked.times, n_channels)
        meeg_values = data.flatten()
        pseudo_participant_ids = np.repeat(channel_names, n_times)
        
        # converting to dataframe
        df = pd.DataFrame({
            "participant": pseudo_participant_ids,
            "time": times,
            "eeg": meeg_values,
            "condition": condition
            })

        all_dfs.append(df)

    return pd.concat(all_dfs, ignore_index=True)

# picking two evoked conditions
faces = evokeds[0]
scrambled = evokeds[1]

# reshaping data by pretending each EEG channel is a participant
reshaped_df = reshape_eeg_channels_as_participants(
    evokeds=[faces, scrambled],
    condition_labels=["faces", "scrambled"]
    )
```

```{python, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
# Load the Python modules
import rpy2.robjects as robjects
from rpy2.robjects.packages import importr
from rpy2.robjects import pandas2ri
from rpy2.robjects.conversion import localconverter

# Import the "neurogam" R package
neurogam = importr("neurogam")

# Assuming reshaped_df is some M/EEG data reshaped in long format
with localconverter(robjects.default_converter + pandas2ri.converter):
    
    reshaped_df_r = robjects.conversion.py2rpy(reshaped_df)
    

# Fit the BGAMM and identify clusters using the testing_through_time() function
gam_onset_offset = neurogam.testing_through_time(
    data=reshaped_df_r,
    threshold=10
    )

# Display the results
print(list(gam_onset_offset) )
```

Similarly, `neurogam` can be called from `Julia` via the `RCall.jl` interface, allowing users to run the same `R` functions from `Julia` workflows without leaving the `Julia` environment.

```{python, eval = FALSE, echo = FALSE}
using RCall
@rimport neurogam

# Assuming reshaped_df is some M/EEG data reshaped in long format
results = neurogam.testing_through_time(data = reshaped_df, threshold = 10)
```

```{.julia}
using RCall
@rimport neurogam

# Assuming reshaped_df is some M/EEG data reshaped in long format
results = neurogam.testing_through_time(data = reshaped_df, threshold = 10)
```
